articleHeader.title: Python Booleans — The Complete Guide

sections.title: What Is a Boolean in Python?

blocks.text: A boolean in Python is a value that represents one of exactly two states: True or False. That's the one-line definition. Here's the version that actually matters once you start writing real code: in Python, bool is not its own independent, self-contained type sitting apart from numbers — it's a subclass of int. True behaves as 1 and False behaves as 0 in every numeric context, and this single design decision quietly explains a whole category of behavior that trips up people coming from languages like Java or C#, where booleans are strictly separate from numbers and can't be added, multiplied, or used as list indices.

Every value in Python, of any type, has an inherent truthiness — a rule for what it evaluates to when Python needs to decide whether it's 'true enough' to satisfy an if, a while, or a boolean operator. This is bigger than the literal True/False keywords: empty lists, empty strings, the number zero, and None are all falsy, while nearly everything else is truthy. This concept — usually called truthiness — is the actual backbone of idiomatic Python conditionals, and it's exactly the part most tutorials gloss over in favor of just showing you if x == True:, which, as we'll get to, is itself a habit worth unlearning.

Here's my honestly opinionated take, upfront, so you can disagree with me for the rest of the article: the boolean concepts most tutorials rush through — truthiness rules for non-boolean types, bool being a subclass of int, and the fact that and/or return actual operand values instead of strict booleans — are exactly the ones that cause production bugs and confusing code review comments. Writing if is_active: instead of if is_active == True: feels like a small stylistic nitpick until you actually understand why the first form is strictly more correct. We're going to spend disproportionate time on that gap.

sections.title: The bool Type — True, False, and bool()

blocks.text: True and False are the two singleton instances of the built-in bool type. They are keywords, always capitalized, and — unlike in Python 2, where you could technically reassign True and False as if they were ordinary variable names in a bizarre historical quirk — Python 3 makes them proper reserved keywords, so any attempt to reassign them is a straightforward SyntaxError. That's a deliberate correctness fix; there was never a good reason to allow True = False to be legal code in the first place.

blocks.label: bool_basics.py
lines: # True and False are reserved keywords in Python 3
# True = 5    # SyntaxError: cannot assign to True

blocks.text: The bool() Constructor — Converting Anything to True or False

The built-in bool() function takes any object and returns its truthiness as an actual bool value. This is the exact function Python calls internally, behind the scenes, every single time it evaluates the condition of an if statement, a while loop, or the operands of and/or. Understanding bool() is really understanding how every conditional in Python actually works under the hood, not just a standalone conversion utility you occasionally call by hand.

blocks.label: bool_constructor.py
lines: print(bool(-5))         # True — any nonzero number is truthy
print(bool('False'))    # True — non-empty string, content doesn't matter
print(bool([0]))        # True — a list containing one item, even a falsy one

blocks.text: That bool('False') being True catches nearly everyone the first time they see it. Python isn't parsing the string's content to check whether it 'means' false — it's only checking whether the string is empty. A non-empty string is truthy no matter what characters it contains, including the literal word 'False,' the digit '0' as text, or a single whitespace character. This exact gotcha shows up constantly in code that reads boolean-looking values from environment variables, config files, or query parameters, where everything arrives as a string, not an actual boolean.

blocks.label: env_var_string_trap.py
lines: # DEBUG=False was set in the environment, but env vars are ALWAYS strings
if debug_flag:                 # BUG: this is True, because 'False' is a non-empty string!
print('Debug mode ON')     # <- this runs even though DEBUG=False was intended
# Correct fix — explicitly compare against the string, or normalize first

blocks.text: I've seen this exact bug ship to production more than once — a feature flag read from an environment variable that was 'off' by every human reading the config file, but 'on' by Python's truthiness rules, because nobody remembered that os.environ.get() always returns a string or None, never an actual boolean.

sections.title: Truthy and Falsy Values — The Real Rulebook

blocks.text: Python defines truthiness for every built-in type, and the rule is consistent across all of them: each type has one canonical 'empty' or 'zero' state that's falsy, and everything else of that type is truthy. Once you see the pattern laid out as a table, it stops being a list of things to memorize and starts being a single rule applied repeatedly.

rows: Truthy by default if neither is defined

blocks.text: Why if my_list: Is More Idiomatic Than if len(my_list) > 0:

Once you trust the truthiness table above, you can write conditionals that read closer to plain English and, in most cases, run measurably faster, because checking whether a container is empty via its inherent truthiness avoids the extra function call and comparison that len(my_list) > 0 requires. This is one of the most common pieces of feedback you'll see in Python code reviews at companies with a strong style culture — not because the longer version is wrong, but because the idiomatic version is both shorter and marginally faster, with zero downside.

blocks.label: truthy_container_check.py
lines: # Idiomatic — relies on the container's own truthiness

blocks.text: Custom Objects — __bool__ and __len__

By default, an instance of a custom class you write is always truthy, no exceptions, unless you explicitly tell Python otherwise. You can control this by defining a __bool__ dunder method on your class, which Python calls whenever your object appears in a boolean context. If you don't define __bool__ but you do define __len__, Python falls back to using __len__ instead, treating a length of zero as falsy — which is exactly why containers like lists and dicts, which define __len__ but not __bool__, are falsy when empty.

blocks.label: custom_bool_dunder.py
lines: print(bool(cart))     # False — falls back to __len__, which is 0
print(bool(cart2))    # True — __len__ returns 1, which is nonzero

sections.title: bool Is a Subclass of int — The Consequences

blocks.text: This is the single fact that unlocks the most 'wait, that actually works?' moments in Python's boolean system. bool inherits directly from int. There is no separate, standalone boolean storage type at the interpreter level — a bool value literally is an int value, restricted to just two instances (True and False), which happen to also print as the words 'True' and 'False' instead of '1' and '0'. This isn't a coincidence or a convenient analogy; it's the actual class hierarchy, and you can verify it directly.

blocks.label: bool_int_subclass.py
lines: print(isinstance(True, int))     # True — bool really is a subclass of int
print(True + True)               # 2 — booleans behave as integers in arithmetic
print(isinstance(True, bool))    # True — still also a bool

blocks.text: Real-World Use: Summing Booleans to Count True Values

This is where the int-subclass fact stops being trivia and becomes a genuinely common, idiomatic pattern. Since True behaves as 1 in arithmetic, you can pass a list (or generator) of booleans straight into sum() to count how many of them are True, without writing a single explicit loop or counter variable. This pattern shows up constantly in data processing, validation summaries, and quick analytics.

blocks.label: sum_booleans.py
lines: print(passing)                  # [False, True, True, True, False, True]
print(num_passing)              # 4 — True counted as 1, False as 0
# Even more common in a single line, no intermediate list needed
num_passing = sum(score >= 60 for score in scores)

blocks.text: The Danger Side: bool as a Dict Key or List Index

The exact same fact that makes the counting trick convenient can also produce genuinely confusing bugs. Because True == 1 and False == 0, using both a boolean and the equivalent integer as dictionary keys silently collides into a single entry, since dictionary key equality is based on == and hash value, and hash(True) == hash(1). This is rare in practice, but it's exactly the kind of thing that produces a baffling, hard-to-reproduce bug when it does happen — usually when a dictionary is built from mixed data sources, some producing actual booleans and others producing 0/1 integers meant to represent the same thing.

blocks.label: bool_dict_collision.py
lines: print(d)              # {True: 'one'} — the second assignment overwrote the first!
print(len(d))         # 1, not 2, because True and 1 hash identically and compare equal
print(d2)             # {False: 'zero'} — same collision with False and 0

blocks.text: Every comparison operator in Python — ==, !=, >, <, >=, <= — evaluates to an actual bool value, which is the most direct and common way boolean values enter your program in the first place. Most real conditionals aren't hand-typed True/False literals; they're the result of some comparison evaluated on the spot.

blocks.label: comparisons_produce_bool.py
lines: # Chained comparisons also produce a single bool

blocks.text: The if x == True: Anti-Pattern

This is a habit worth actively unlearning, and it's flagged by essentially every Python linter for good reason. If x is already a boolean expression or a variable holding a boolean, writing if x == True: is redundant — if x: does exactly the same thing, more directly, without an unnecessary comparison. Worse, == True is actually less correct in an important edge case: because bool is a subclass of int, a value like the integer 1 is truthy but 1 == True also happens to be True, which can mask type confusion; meanwhile a value like a non-empty string is truthy but 'some text' == True is False, meaning the == True version would silently reject a genuinely truthy value that if x: would have correctly accepted.

blocks.label: equals_true_antipattern.py
lines: is_active = 'yes'    # imagine this came from a truthy-but-non-boolean source
print('Not active')     # <- WRONG output: 'yes' is truthy, but != True
print('Active')         # <- CORRECT: relies on actual truthiness

blocks.text: The PEP 8 style guide is explicit about this: comparisons to singletons like True, False, and None should always use is/is not or plain truthiness, never ==. The one narrow exception is when you genuinely need to distinguish a real bool from a truthy non-boolean value — for example, validating that a JSON field is strictly true/false and not some other truthy value like 1 or a non-empty string — in which case is True or an explicit isinstance(x, bool) check is the correct, intentional tool, not an accident.

sections.title: Logical Operators — and, or, not on Booleans

blocks.text: Python's logical operators — and, or, not — are how you combine boolean expressions, and they use short-circuit evaluation: Python stops evaluating as soon as the overall result is already determined, skipping any remaining operands entirely. This isn't just a speed optimization; it's used deliberately as a control-flow tool throughout real Python code.

blocks.label: logical_operators_bool.py
lines: print(has_email)                    # None — safely short-circuits, no crash

blocks.text: and/or Don't Always Return an Actual Boolean

This is the exact same surprise from the operators guide, worth repeating here because it's specifically about booleans and easy to misjudge. and and or return one of their actual operand values, not necessarily True/False. and returns the first falsy operand it finds, or the last operand if everything is truthy. or returns the first truthy operand it finds, or the last operand if everything is falsy. Only when both operands genuinely are booleans do you reliably get a bool back.

blocks.label: logical_return_values.py
lines: print(True and False)         # False — both are real booleans, so result is bool
print('' or 'default')        # 'default' — a string, not True/False
print(0 and 5)                 # 0 — a number, not False

blocks.text: That last pattern, value = user_input or 'default', is genuinely idiomatic and shows up constantly for supplying a fallback value — but be careful with it whenever a legitimately meaningful falsy value (like the number 0, or an empty list that's a valid, intentional result) could show up as user_input. In that case, the or fallback pattern quietly overwrites a real, valid value with the default, which is a subtle logic bug, not a crash — the kind that survives testing and only shows up against real data. If zero or an empty container is a legitimate value you need to preserve, use value = user_input if user_input is not None else 'default' instead.

sections.title: How Python Evaluates Truthiness in a Conditional — Visual Flow

blocks.text: Because if, while, and the logical operators all funnel through the exact same truthiness machinery, it helps to see the actual decision path Python follows any time it needs to decide whether a value counts as true. The diagram below traces that path from the raw value all the way to the branch Python actually takes.

blocks.title: Python Truthiness Evaluation: Value → bool() → Branch Taken
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
    A[Value used in if / while / and / or\ne.g. if x:] --> B{Is it already a bool?}
    B -->|Yes, True or False| C[Use directly]
    B -->|No| D{Does the type define __bool__?}
    D -->|Yes| E[Call __bool__\nreturns True or False]
    D -->|No| F{Does the type define __len__?}
    F -->|Yes| G[Call __len__\nlen == 0 -> False\nlen > 0 -> True]
    F -->|No| H[Default: always True\nno emptiness concept]
    C --> I{Result}
    E --> I
    G --> I
    H --> I
    I -->|True| J[Branch taken\nif-body runs / loop continues]
    I -->|False| K[Branch skipped\nelse runs / loop exits]

blocks.text: The two branches worth internalizing: first, plain numbers and strings never define __bool__ themselves — their truthiness is actually handled by CPython's built-in type implementations directly, but conceptually it follows the exact same __len__/zero-check pattern shown here. Second, for your own custom classes, if you define neither __bool__ nor __len__, Python takes the rightmost path and treats every instance as truthy, unconditionally — which is exactly why forgetting to define either one on a container-like custom class can produce an object that reports itself as truthy even when it's logically empty.

sections.title: Membership and Identity Operators — Also Produce Booleans

blocks.text: Two more operator families round out where boolean values come from in everyday Python: membership (in, not in) and identity (is, is not). Both always evaluate to a genuine bool, unlike and/or, which makes them safe to use directly inside further boolean logic or to store as-is without worrying about the 'returns an operand, not a bool' surprise.

blocks.label: membership_identity_bool.py
lines: print(is_missing)             # True — always a real bool, never an operand echo

blocks.text: Why is None Is the Correct Boolean-Adjacent Check, Not == None

This is directly tied to the boolean discussion because checking for None is one of the most common conditional checks in any real codebase, and it's frequently written incorrectly. None is a true singleton — there is exactly one None object in the entire running program — so identity comparison with is is both faster and more correct than value comparison with ==, because is can never be overridden by a custom __eq__ method on some other class, while == theoretically can, producing surprising results if a class's equality method doesn't handle comparison against None sensibly.

sections.title: Python Booleans vs Java and JavaScript

blocks.text: If you move between languages regularly, this table saves you the 'wait, why does 5 && 3 not give me a real boolean here' moment during a live coding round.

rows: boolean, primitive, NOT related to int
[] is truthy! (only '', 0, null, undefined, NaN are falsy)

blocks.text: The row worth pausing on if you're switching from JavaScript: an empty array [] is truthy in JavaScript, but an empty list [] is falsy in Python. This exact difference has caused real bugs for developers moving between a Node.js backend and a Python data pipeline in the same week, where a guard clause that worked correctly in one language silently does the opposite in the other.

sections.title: Where Boolean Concepts Actually Show Up in Real Codebases

blocks.text: Booleans aren't just interview fodder — here's where you'll genuinely run into each concept once you're working on real projects, not just tutorial exercises.

items.text: — if not user or not user.is_active: return is one of the most common lines in any web framework's view or route handler, relying entirely on truthiness rather than explicit comparisons.

items.strong: sum() over boolean generators for analytics
items.text: — sum(order.is_refunded for order in orders) to quickly count how many orders in a batch match a condition, no explicit loop needed.
— every config-loading module needs explicit string-to-boolean normalization, since env vars and most config file formats deliver strings, not real booleans.

items.strong: Default values with the or pattern
items.text: — timeout = config.get('timeout') or 30 is everywhere in library and framework code, though it requires care around legitimately falsy valid values.
— a Cart, Queue, or Batch class defining __bool__ or __len__ so if cart: reads naturally as 'if the cart has anything in it.'

items.strong: is None checks in API and ORM code
items.text: — distinguishing 'field was not provided' (None) from 'field was explicitly set to a falsy value' (0, '', False) is a constant theme in API validation and database query building.
— JSON schema validators and API input checkers that need to reject 1 or 'true' as invalid substitutes for an actual boolean field, relying on the fact that bool is technically also an int.

sections.title: Do's and Don'ts With Python Booleans

blocks.text: A quick reference for the habits that separate code that works from code that works AND doesn't produce a confusing bug three sprints from now.

pros.title: Rely on truthiness directly: if x: not if x == True:
pros.text: It's shorter, faster, and more correct — == True can reject genuinely truthy non-boolean values.

pros.title: Use is None / is not None for null checks
pros.text: None is a true singleton; identity comparison is both faster and immune to custom __eq__ surprises.

pros.title: Use sum() over a boolean generator to count matches
pros.text: Leverages bool being an int subclass for clean, loop-free counting logic.

pros.title: Define __bool__ or __len__ on container-like custom classes
pros.text: Without either, your objects are always truthy by default, even when logically empty.

pros.title: Normalize string-based flags explicitly
pros.text: Environment variables and config values are strings — always compare explicitly (e.g. .lower() == 'true') rather than relying on their truthiness.

pros.title: Use isinstance(x, bool) when you need a strict boolean check
pros.text: Necessary any time 1 or 'true' should NOT be silently accepted as a valid boolean, given bool's int subclass relationship.

cons.title: Don't compare booleans with == True or == False
cons.text: Flagged by most linters; use direct truthiness or is for singleton checks instead.

cons.title: Don't assume and/or always return an actual bool
cons.text: They return operand values — only genuinely reliable as strict booleans when both operands already are booleans.

cons.title: Don't use the `x or default` pattern when 0, '', or [] are valid values
cons.text: It silently overwrites legitimate falsy values with the fallback — use an explicit is None check instead.

cons.title: Don't mix bool and int as dictionary keys expecting separate entries
cons.text: True/1 and False/0 hash identically and will silently collide into a single key.

cons.title: Don't forget that an empty list/dict/string is falsy
cons.text: Especially relevant if you're used to JavaScript, where empty arrays and objects are truthy.

blocks.text: These come up constantly, whether it's a fresher round at a service company or a mid-level screen at a product startup. Know the reasoning behind the answer, not just the answer itself — interviewers almost always ask a follow-up 'why'.

items.q: Q1. Is bool a separate type from int in Python?
items.a: No, not at the class-hierarchy level. bool is defined as a subclass of int, with exactly two instances, True and False, which behave as 1 and 0 respectively in any numeric context. isinstance(True, int) returns True, and True + True evaluates to 2. bool is still its own distinct type for isinstance checks and display purposes, but it inherits int's arithmetic behavior directly.

items.q: Q2. What values are falsy in Python besides False itself?
items.a: None, the number zero in any numeric type (0, 0.0, 0j), and any empty container or sequence — '', [], (), {}, and set(). Every other value, including any non-empty string (even 'False' or '0' as text) and any non-empty container, is truthy by default.

items.q: Q3. Why is if x == True: considered bad practice?
items.a: It's redundant when x is already boolean-like, since if x: does the same thing more directly. Worse, it's actually less correct than plain truthiness in an edge case: a truthy non-boolean value like a non-empty string or the integer 2 would satisfy if x: but fail x == True, since only the literal value 1 equals True numerically. PEP 8 recommends direct truthiness checks or is comparisons for singletons instead.

items.q: Q4. What does sum([True, False, True, True]) return, and why?
items.a: It returns 3. Since bool is a subclass of int, True is treated as 1 and False as 0 in any arithmetic context, including inside sum(). This makes sum() over a list or generator of boolean values a common, idiomatic way to count how many elements satisfy some condition.

items.q: Q5. Why can {True: 'a', 1: 'b'} end up with only one key?
items.a: Because dictionary keys are compared using both hash value and equality, and hash(True) == hash(1) while True == 1, Python treats them as the same key. The second assignment overwrites the first, leaving a dictionary with a single entry, {True: 'b'}, rather than two separate entries.

items.q: Q6. What's the difference between is None and == None for checking null values?
items.a: is None checks object identity against the single None singleton, which is fast and can never be overridden by a custom class's equality logic. == None relies on the __eq__ method, which a poorly written custom class could override in a way that produces unexpected results when compared to None. PEP 8 explicitly recommends is None / is not None for this reason.

items.q: Q7. Does the expression '' or 'default' return a boolean?
items.a: No. or returns one of its actual operand values, not necessarily True or False. Since the empty string is falsy, or moves on to evaluate and return the second operand, 'default', which is a string, not a boolean. Only when both operands are already genuine booleans is the result guaranteed to be a bool.

items.q: Q8. Why is an empty list falsy in Python but truthy in JavaScript?
items.a: This is a language design difference, not a universal rule. Python defines truthiness for containers based on emptiness via the __len__ mechanism — an empty list has length 0, so it's falsy. JavaScript's truthiness rules only mark a small fixed set of values as falsy (0, '', null, undefined, NaN, false), and objects/arrays, even empty ones, are always truthy because they're reference types checked for existence, not content.

items.q: Q9. What happens if you define __len__ but not __bool__ on a custom class?
items.a: Python falls back to __len__ to determine truthiness: if __len__ returns 0, the object is falsy; any nonzero length makes it truthy. If neither __bool__ nor __len__ is defined, instances of the class are always truthy, regardless of their internal state.

items.q: Q10. How do you strictly validate that a value is a real boolean and not just truthy?
items.a: Use isinstance(x, bool) rather than a plain truthiness check. Because bool is a subclass of int, values like 1 or 0 would pass a naive truthiness test intended for actual booleans, and isinstance(x, int) alone would incorrectly accept real booleans too. isinstance(x, bool) combined with type(x) is bool (for excluding subclassing edge cases) is the precise way to check.

blocks.text: Try to answer each one mentally before checking. If you get one wrong, that's exactly the kind of gap that turns into a real bug later — worth re-reading that section above.

items.q: 1. What does bool('0') return, and why does this surprise people?
items.a: It returns True. bool() on a string only checks whether the string is empty or not — it never inspects the string's content. '0' is a single-character, non-empty string, so it's truthy, even though the character it contains looks like it should mean 'false' or 'zero' to a human reader.

items.q: 2. What is the output of print(True + True + False)?
items.a: 2. Because bool is a subclass of int, True behaves as 1 and False as 0 in arithmetic. True + True + False evaluates as 1 + 1 + 0, which is 2.

items.q: 3. Why might quantity = form_data.get('quantity') or 1 introduce a bug?
items.a: If the user legitimately submits a quantity of 0 (a valid, meaningful falsy value), the or operator treats 0 as falsy and silently substitutes the fallback value 1 instead of preserving the user's actual input. The safer version explicitly checks for None: quantity = form_data.get('quantity') if form_data.get('quantity') is not None else 1.

items.q: 4. What does isinstance(True, int) return, and what does that reveal about Python's type system?
items.a: It returns True, revealing that bool is implemented as a subclass of int in CPython's type hierarchy, not as an entirely separate primitive type the way it is in many other languages. This is why booleans can participate directly in arithmetic without any implicit conversion.

items.q: 5. What is the output of print(not not 'hello')?
items.a: True. The inner not converts the truthy non-empty string 'hello' to False (its negation), and the outer not flips that back to True. Double-not is actually a common, legitimate idiom for explicitly coercing any value to a strict boolean, functionally equivalent to calling bool() directly.

items.q: 6. Why does {}  evaluate as falsy, but a class instance with no attributes set evaluate as truthy by default?
items.a: {} is an empty dict, a built-in type whose __len__ returns 0, making it falsy by Python's container truthiness rules. A plain custom class instance, unless it explicitly defines __bool__ or __len__, has no built-in notion of 'emptiness' at all — Python's default fallback for any object without those dunder methods is to treat it as always truthy, regardless of what attributes it does or doesn't have set.

items.q: 7. What does list(map(bool, [0, 1, '', 'a', None, [1]])) return?
items.a: [False, True, False, True, False, True]. Each element is passed through bool(): 0 is falsy, 1 is truthy, '' (empty string) is falsy, 'a' (non-empty string) is truthy, None is falsy, and [1] (non-empty list) is truthy.

items.q: 8. Why does 5 == 5.0 and 5 is not 5.0 both return True in Python?
items.a: == checks value equality, and Python compares numeric types across int/float by their mathematical value, so 5 (an int) and 5.0 (a float) are considered equal in content. is checks identity — whether both names point to the exact same object in memory — and since int and float are different types stored as different objects, they can never be the same object, so is correctly returns False (making 'is not' True) even though their values are mathematically equal.

sections.title: Conclusion — Booleans Look Trivial Until the Edge Cases Show Up

blocks.text: Booleans are usually presented as the simplest possible data type any language offers — just two values, what could go wrong? In Python specifically, quite a bit, precisely because bool isn't quarantined off from the rest of the type system the way it is in many other languages. It's a full participant in arithmetic, it's woven into every container's notion of truthiness, and the logical operators built around it return actual values rather than a sanitized True/False result. That's not a design flaw — it's a deliberate, coherent system — but it does mean that treating bool as 'just true or false, nothing more to know' is exactly the mindset that produces the bugs covered throughout this guide.

If there's one habit worth building from this entire guide, it's this: whenever you write a conditional, pause for a second and ask what's actually being evaluated for truthiness — a real boolean, a number, a string, a container, or a custom object — and whether Python's default truthiness rule for that type is actually the rule your logic depends on. That two-second pause is cheaper than the debugging session you'll otherwise have three sprints from now, when a feature flag read as a string, or a fallback value that quietly swallowed a legitimate zero, is buried inside a much bigger function nobody remembers writing that way on purpose.

Designing domain models or container-like classes

blocks.text: Next, take these boolean concepts into actual control-flow structures — if/elif/else, while loops, and comprehensions with filter conditions — where they combine constantly with the operators and truthiness rules covered here. That's where booleans stop being 'the type with two values' and start being the quiet logic underneath nearly every decision your program makes.

items.q: Is bool a primitive type in Python like it is in Java or C?
items.a: No. Python doesn't have primitive types in the Java/C sense at all — everything, including booleans, is a full object. bool is specifically implemented as a subclass of int, with exactly two instances, True and False, meaning it inherits integer arithmetic behavior rather than being isolated as its own unrelated type.

items.q: What is the difference between True and 1 in Python?
items.a: They are equal in value (True == 1 is True) and True is even an instance of int, but they are still distinguishable: type(True) is bool while type(1) is int, and isinstance(True, bool) is True while isinstance(1, bool) is False. For most practical purposes they behave identically in arithmetic, but strict type checks can and do tell them apart.

items.q: Why does an empty string evaluate to False in an if statement?
items.a: Python defines truthiness for strings based on whether they're empty or not. An empty string '' has zero length and is treated as falsy, exactly the same way an empty list or empty dict is falsy. Any non-empty string, regardless of its actual content, is truthy.

items.q: Can you use and/or/not as if they always return True or False?
items.a: not always returns a strict boolean. and and or do not — they return one of their actual operand values rather than a sanitized True/False. If you need a guaranteed strict boolean result from a compound expression, wrap it explicitly in bool(), e.g. bool(a or b).

items.q: How do you check if a variable is exactly True, not just truthy?
items.a: Use is True, e.g. if value is True:. This is an identity check against the actual True singleton, and it will correctly reject other truthy values like 1, 'yes', or a non-empty list, which if value: alone would accept. This distinction matters mainly when parsing strict boolean fields from external data like JSON.

items.q: Why do Python booleans print as True and False instead of 1 and 0?
items.a: Because bool overrides the display behavior it inherits from int with its own __repr__/__str__, so printing or displaying a bool value shows the word 'True' or 'False' rather than the underlying numeric value, even though arithmetic operations still treat it as 1 or 0 under the hood.
